summary: Umar says he does not mind whether his morning brings what he likes or what he dislikes, since he does not know where the good lies.

Hasan reports that Ali was told Abu Dharr prefers poverty and illness; Ali replies that whoever relies on Allaah's choice never wishes for another state, and separately says that whoever is content with Allaah's decision is rewarded.
notes: Two sayings of Ali: his reply about Abu Dharr, then a separate statement introduced with 'It was also Hadhrat Ali'.

summary: Abdullaah bin Mas'ood says that on the Day of Qiyaamah people will wish they had only enough food to live on, that daily conditions harm only a heart full of anger, and that it is better to burn oneself than to say 'if only' about what Allaah has decreed.
Kumayl bin Ziyaad relates that at a graveyard Ali addressed the dead, told Kumayl that the best provision is taqwa, and wept, saying the grave is a box holding one's actions.
Qais bin Abu Haazim reports Ali's advice to value the acceptance of one's deeds above taqwa itself.
Another report gives Ali saying that a deed done with taqwa can never be undermined, so how can an accepted deed ever be undermined.
Abdullaah bin Mas'ood says that knowing Allaah has accepted even one of his deeds is dearer to him than earth full of gold.
Abu Dardaa says the sleep of the intelligent and the little good done with taqwa and conviction are worth more than a mountain of worship by the negligent.
Abu Dardaa says that knowing for certain that Allaah accepted one of his salaah is dearer to him than the whole world, citing the verse that Allaah accepts only from those with taqwa.

Ubay bin Ka'b says that whoever gives up something for Allaah's pleasure is given something better from unexpected sources, while the careless who take without knowing the lawful source are afflicted.
Abdullaah bin Abbaas reports that Abu Bakr and then Umar each noticed the Prophet's greying hair, and the Prophet said Surah Hood and the surahs with it had whitened it.
notes: Two versions of the same incident: Abu Bakr's remark, then Umar's.

summary: Abu Sa'eed reports the Prophet's concern about the angel ready to blow the Trumpet and the words he taught the Sahabah in reply; Abdullaah bin Umar reports that the Prophet fainted on hearing a verse about the chains of Jahannam.
notes: Two reports (Abu Sa'eed, then Abdullaah bin Umar). The trailing heading 'The Fear of the Sahabah' looks like section-title debris from the next section.

summary: Sahl bin Sa'd reports that a young Ansaari, overcome by fear of Jahannam, died in the Prophet's embrace, and the Prophet ordered him enshrouded because fear had ruptured his liver.
Hudhayfah reports the same incident: the youth stood to embrace the Prophet and fell dead, and the Prophet said Allaah had saved him from the Fire and that whoever fears something will flee from it.

Abdullaah bin Abbaas reports that when the verse about saving yourselves from the Fire was recited, a young Sahabi fainted; the Prophet told him to say Laa Ilaaha illallaah and gave him glad tidings of Jannah.

Sa'eed bin Musayyib reports the Prophet's visit to the ill Umar, who said he had both hope and fear; Hasan reports Abu Bakr saying that Allaah pairs ease with hardship so the believer keeps both hope and fear.
notes: Two reports: Sa'eed bin Musayyib on Umar's illness, then Hasan on Abu Bakr's words.

summary: Abdullaah bin Roomi reports that Uthmaan said he would rather be turned to ashes than not know whether he is going to Jannah or Jahannam.
Qataadah reports three wishes: Abu Ubaydah wished to be a sheep that is slaughtered and eaten, and Imraan bin Husayn wished to be sand that the wind blows away.
notes: Three separate sayings, all reported by Qataadah.

summary: Aamir bin Masrooq reports that Abdullaah bin Mas'ood, told that someone did not want to be among the As'haabul Yameen, said he himself wished not to be resurrected at all; Hasan reports Abdullaah saying he would rather be dust than be placed between Jannah and Jahannam.
notes: Two reports: Aamir bin Masrooq's, then Hasan's. The quoted saying is cut off in the source ('the ...').

summary: Abu Dharr says that if people knew what he knew they would neglect their wives and beds, and wishes Allaah had created him as a felled tree whose fruit is eaten.
Hizaam bin Hakeem reports Abu Dardaa saying that if people knew what follows death they would take no pleasure in food or drink, and wishing to be a felled tree.
Abu Dardaa wishes to be a sheep whose throat is cut to feed guests, and Abdullaah bin Umar wishes to be a pillar.
notes: Two separate sayings (Abu Dardaa, then Abdullaah bin Umar).

summary: Tawoos reports that Mu'aadh bin Jabal refused to let scholars build him a masjid, fearing to carry it on the Day of Qiyaamah; Naafi and Abu Haazim report Abdullaah bin Umar's fear of Allaah in sajdah and his remark on a man who fell unconscious at the recitation of the Qur'aan.
notes: Several reports (Tawoos, Naafi, Abu Haazim). The Naafi passage breaks off mid-sentence in the source.

summary: Shaddaad bin Aws Ansaari, unable to sleep from fear of Jahannam, would cry out to Allaah and then stand in salaah until morning.

Amr bin Salamah reports Aa'isha wishing she were a tree or sand, or had never been created; another report has Abdullaah bin Abbaas praising Aa'isha before her death, and she replies that she wishes only to be forgotten.
notes: Two reports. The second names Abdullaah bin Abbaas as the one praising Aa'isha, but her reply refers to Abdullaah bin Umar; the source may be garbled.

summary: Abdullaah bin Mas'ood reports that the Prophet asked him to recite the Qur'aan, and that when he reached the verse about a witness from every nation the Prophet's eyes filled with tears and he said that was enough.
Abu Hurayrah reports that the men of Suffa wept when a verse was revealed, the Prophet wept with them, and he said the one who weeps out of fear of Allaah will never enter Jahannam.

Anas reports the Prophet describing the fire of Jahannam and an Abyssinian man weeping loudly before him; the Prophet praised him, and Allaah's message brought through Jibra'eel is that tears shed in fear of Him will be rewarded with laughter in Jannah.
Qais bin Abu Haazim says that when he went to visit the Prophet he found Abu Bakr had already taken his place as Khalifah, and that Abu Bakr praised Allaah at length in his address and wept greatly.

Hasan bin Muhammad bin Abi Taalib reports that Umar wept so much reciting Surah Takweer in the Friday sermon that his voice stopped, and that after reciting Surah Toor he fell ill and people visited him for twenty days.

people.name: Hasan bin Muhammad bin Abi Taalib

notes: Two separate incidents (Surah Takweer, then Surah Toor). The narrator's name is garbled in the source; the name given is the best the text supports.

summary: Ubayd bin Umayr Laythi reports that Umar wept while leading Fajr with Surah Yusuf, stopped at the verse about Ya'qoob's eyes whitening with sorrow, and then bowed into ruku.
Abdullaah bin Shaddaad bin Haad says he could hear Umar sobbing in the Fajr prayer from the last rows, as Umar recited Surah Yusuf and stopped at the verse about complaining of sorrow to Allaah.
Hishaam bin Hasan narrates that a verse sometimes choked Umar with emotion, so that he would fall down weeping and stay indoors while people visited him thinking he was ill.
Haani, freed slave of Uthmaan, reports that Uthmaan wept at graveyards, quoting the Prophet that the grave is the first stage of the Aakhirah and the most frightening sight he had seen.

Abdullaah bin Umar reports that Umar asked the weeping Mu'aadh bin Jabal why he wept, and Mu'aadh quoted the Prophet that even slight ostentation is shirk and that the people most beloved to Allaah are the hidden God-fearing.

Abdullaah bin Umar wept so much reciting Surah Mutaffifeen that he fell down; Naafi reports he always wept at certain verses of Baqarah and Hadeed; Yusuf bin Maahak reports walking with Abdullaah bin Umar to ask about Abu Dharr's worship, which was meditation in solitude.
notes: Several reports. The Yusuf bin Maahak passage breaks off mid-sentence in the source, and the woman who answers is not named.

summary: Aun bin Abdullaah bin Utba reports that Ummu Dardaa named meditation and heeding lessons as Abu Dardaa's best deed, and Abu Dardaa said meditation for a moment is better than standing in salaah all night.
notes: Three versions of Ummu Dardaa's answer, then Abu Dardaa's own saying.

summary: Abu Dardaa says some people are keys to good and locks to evil, who will be richly rewarded, while others are keys to evil and locks to good, who will be severely punished, and repeats that meditation for a moment is better than a night of salaah.

Habeeb bin Abdullaah reports Abu Dardaa advising a man going to jihaad to remember Allaah in ease so that He remembers him in hardship; Saalim bin Abil Ja'd reports Abu Dardaa drawing a lesson from two bulls, one whipped for stopping and the other spared.
notes: Two reports: Habeeb's account of the advice, then Saalim's report of the two bulls.

summary: A freed slave of Abu Bakr reports Abu Bakr saying that whoever opposes his own carnal self for Allaah's sake will be saved from Allaah's anger.
